utterances.text: I think manufacturers should be required to sell replacement parts and repair manuals, because independent repairers can fix modern devices without them.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: But a mandatory supply rule would force small manufacturers to stock parts for years, and that could ruin them.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: In other words, Nkechi, you want a legal duty on every manufacturer, big or small, to supply parts and manuals.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Side note: my laptop hinge snapped last week, so I am reading this thread with some bitterness.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Another worry is that untrained battery repair is a real fire risk, since fire services report battery fires caused by botched home repairs.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Rafael, is that home repair can burn houses down.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Put another way, people without training risk starting battery fires when they repair devices.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: By the way, the mods renamed this thread overnight.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Still, repair should be made easier, and recycling alone is not enough. Repair being made easier is the reason that people without training risk starting battery fires when they repair devices, as Ivana said.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: I would back both of those, since electronic waste is the fastest-growing waste stream.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Welcome to the programme. Tonight's question: should mobile operating systems be required to allow alternative app stores? Rashid, you first.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Yes, because a single store owner takes thirty percent of every sale, a toll that developers simply cannot avoid.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Alternative stores would also push commission fees down, since developers could move their apps to cheaper stores.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Ulla, your response?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: But the curated store keeps malware out, and that matters more than fees, since last year ninety-eight percent of detected malware came from outside official stores.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: That ignores the fact that one major system already allows sideloading, and its users are not infected in great numbers. I carry phones on both systems, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: So you are saying the system that allows alternative stores has not suffered mass infection?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Small developers lose the most under today's rules, which is another reason to open the market. Put another way, the fee hits the smallest studios hardest.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Alternative stores also mean users must judge each store themselves, because nobody would be the one party in charge of checking apps.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: In other words, Ulla, ordinary users would be left to vet stores alone?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Users already vet apps by reading reviews.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The European rule came into force this spring.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Vetting stores would be no great leap for users.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: So, Rashid, you are saying cheaper rival stores would force the commission down?

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: And Ulla, what you mean is that malware risk outweighs the relief from lower fees? Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Welcome to the programme. Tonight's question: should mobile operating systems be required to allow alternative app stores? Rashid, you first.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Yes, because a single store owner takes thirty percent of every sale, a toll that developers simply cannot avoid.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Alternative stores would also push commission fees down, since developers could move their apps to cheaper stores.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Ulla, your response?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: But the curated store keeps malware out, and that matters more than fees, since last year ninety-eight percent of detected malware came from outside official stores.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: That ignores the fact that one major system already allows sideloading, and its users are not infected in great numbers. I carry phones on both systems, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: So you are saying the system that allows alternative stores has not suffered mass infection?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Small developers lose the most under today's rules, which is another reason to open the market. Put another way, the fee hits the smallest studios hardest.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Alternative stores also mean users must judge each store themselves, because no single party would be responsible for checking apps.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: In other words, Ulla, ordinary users would be left to vet stores alone?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Mobile operating systems should be required to allow alternative app stores; in other words, vetting stores would be no great leap for users, because users already vet apps by reading reviews, since, as Ulla says, users must judge the trustworthiness of each store themselves.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The European rule came into force this spring.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Most app stores list their apps in dozens of languages.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: So, Rashid, you are saying cheaper rival stores would force the commission down?

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: And Ulla, what you mean is that malware risk outweighs the relief from lower fees? Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Welcome to the programme. Tonight's question: should mobile operating systems be required to allow alternative app stores? Rashid, you first.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Yes, because a single store owner takes thirty percent of every sale, a toll that developers simply cannot avoid.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Alternative stores would also push commission fees down, since developers could move their apps to cheaper stores.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Ulla, your response?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: But the curated store keeps malware out, and that matters more than fees, since last year ninety-eight percent of detected malware came from outside official stores.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: That ignores the fact that one major system already allows sideloading, and its users are not infected in great numbers. I carry phones on both systems, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: So you are saying the system that allows alternative stores has not suffered mass infection?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Small developers lose the most under today's rules, which is another reason to open the market. Put another way, the fee hits the smallest studios hardest.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Alternative stores also mean users must judge each store themselves, because no single party would be responsible for checking apps.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: In other words, Ulla, ordinary users would be left to vet stores alone?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Users already vet apps by reading reviews, which is why vetting stores is no great leap, and that is why the requirement should stand.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The European rule came into force this spring.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: So, Rashid, you are saying alternative stores would push commission fees down, because cheaper rival stores would force the commission down?

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: And Ulla, what you mean is that malware risk outweighs the relief from lower fees? Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether annual bonuses should depend more on team performance than individual targets. Petra, could you start us off?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Team members often possess complementary expertise.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: For that reason, annual bonuses should depend more on team performance than on individual targets.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: But team-based bonuses can conceal free riders. That risk makes me cautious about shifting the balance.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Individual targets can reward employees for optimizing their own tasks rather than helping colleagues; that is another reason to give team performance more weight.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: A shared bonus gives employees a financial reason to rescue a delayed teammate.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Cooperation across departments is also a reason to give team performance more weight in annual bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Managers can use peer reviews to identify unusual individual contributions. Therefore, individual targets do not need to be the sole measure of performance.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Team metrics are harder to compare across projects. As a result, individual targets are more precise than team metrics in some situations.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: A team may miss its deadline because another department supplied data late. This shows that team results can reflect dependencies outside a team's control.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Employees often cover for absent colleagues, which supports recognizing collective results in annual bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: In other words, bonuses should recognize what colleagues achieve together; even so, bonuses should retain an individual component.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: In other words, a stronger team component would reward cooperation across departments.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: To put the balance plainly, individual targets should not be the sole basis of annual bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The finance committee will review the bonus budget next month.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I have already drafted a possible bonus-calculation spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our question is whether criminal trials for every serious offence should require a unanimous jury verdict. Magnus, begin with you.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A single juror can block a verdict under a unanimous-jury rule. Because that one-person veto can leave a case unresolved, unanimity makes hung trials more likely.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Unanimity gives every juror an equal voice. That safeguard matters especially when the charge carries a severe sentence.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Yara, does the possibility of a hung trial outweigh that safeguard?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Several legal systems permit qualified-majority jury verdicts. Since those systems recognize such verdicts, a qualified-majority jury verdict can still be lawful.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Jury deliberations often expose weaknesses in the evidence. That is why requiring unanimity would improve the accuracy of serious-offence verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, what is the practical cost when a jury cannot agree?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Hung trials force victims to endure another legal proceeding. Because avoiding unnecessary retrials is valuable, that is a reason not to demand unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel has now raised fairness, accuracy, and the burden of retrials. Yara, where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I am concerned that a narrow majority could convict someone despite serious doubts. The courthouse in my district has two jury rooms.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: I once served on a jury. Majority verdicts can reflect careful jury deliberation.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Serious offences should not require unanimous jury verdicts; because of that, unanimity makes hung trials more likely.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: But that conclusion is mistaken: serious offences deserve the strongest protection against wrongful conviction.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: In other words, Chidi's point is that unanimity gives every juror an equal voice.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So Chidi's position is that a qualified-majority jury verdict can still be lawful.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Put another way, Seamus's position is that majority verdicts can still reflect careful jury deliberation.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I once attended a jury trial as a member of the public.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The jury pool for serious-offence trials is drawn from the whole county.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our question is whether criminal trials for every serious offence should require a unanimous jury verdict. Magnus, begin with you.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A single juror can block a verdict under a unanimous-jury rule. Because that one-person veto can leave a case unresolved, unanimity makes hung trials more likely.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Unanimity gives every juror an equal voice. That safeguard matters especially when the charge carries a severe sentence.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Yara, does the possibility of a hung trial outweigh that safeguard?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: A qualified-majority jury verdict can still be lawful. Since such a verdict can still be lawful, several legal systems permit qualified-majority jury verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Jury deliberations often expose weaknesses in the evidence. That is why requiring unanimity would improve the accuracy of serious-offence verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, what is the practical cost when a jury cannot agree?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Hung trials force victims to endure another legal proceeding. Because avoiding unnecessary retrials is valuable, that is a reason not to demand unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel has now raised fairness, accuracy, and the burden of retrials. Yara, where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I am concerned that a narrow majority could convict someone despite serious doubts. The courthouse in my district has two jury rooms.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: I once served on a jury. Majority verdicts can reflect careful jury deliberation.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Serious offences should not require unanimous jury verdicts. Since serious offences should not require unanimous jury verdicts, a unanimous-jury rule makes hung trials more likely.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: But that conclusion is mistaken: serious offences deserve the strongest protection against wrongful conviction.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: In other words, Chidi's point is that unanimity gives every juror an equal voice.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So Chidi's position is that a qualified-majority jury verdict can still be lawful.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Put another way, Seamus's position is that majority verdicts can still reflect careful jury deliberation.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I once attended a jury trial as a member of the public.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should governments cap the fees that payment processors charge small businesses? Anika, you start.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Yes. Governments should put a ceiling on those fees, because fees of about 2.5 percent take half the profit of a typical small shop.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Why half?

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Since typical small-shop profit margins are only about five percent.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: I ran a bakery for ten years before moving into consulting.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: But a cap would make processors drop small merchants, because serving them would be unprofitable under a cap.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: So you are saying small shops would lose the ability to accept cards.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Yes, and that would hurt, because shops that cannot take cards lose customers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Sanna, you disagree with both of them?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: A cap is the wrong tool; transparency rules would work better, since small merchants cannot meaningfully compare processors' prices today.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: In other words, small firms cannot shop around, because termination fees run to several hundred pounds.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Those fees bite hard since the contracts run for three years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Anika, can you pull that together?

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Put another way, shops are locked in for years, which happens because the contracts renew automatically.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Renewal really is automatic in practice, since the window for cancelling is only thirty days, which is the case because termination fees run to several hundred pounds.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We are nearly out of time. Sanna, a final word.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Only that the finance ministry publishes its review of card fees next spring.

utterances.text: But traditional report cards provide families with a written record of student progress, and that is why I object to replacing them entirely.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Many parents have difficulty finding time for school appointments. The policy would need to account for that practical issue.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Because schools should use twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences instead of traditional report cards, schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: I think professional basketball teams should be required to disclose players' injury details before every game. Pre-game injury information helps fans decide whether a game is worth watching, which is one reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I disagree with requiring that disclosure because it could expose players' private medical information.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: The rule could be narrower: teams could report each player's injury status and expected availability without publishing a full medical diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: So you are proposing a report limited to injury status and expected availability.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Exactly. A limited injury report would protect players' privacy while giving the public useful information, which is why teams should still be required to provide it. The arena's roof was repaired last summer.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Exact medical diagnoses add little to fans' decisions about attending or watching a game; that is another reason to require a public availability report.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: In other words, my proposal is for a status-and-availability report rather than a medical file.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Teams already collect player-availability information for internal game planning, which is another reason to require them to disclose it before games. I have attended three professional basketball games this month.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: A public injury report also helps opposing teams prepare for the game, which is a further reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: So you are saying that every team should publish a limited injury report before each game.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether supermarkets should stop offering plastic produce bags. Selin, you start.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Supermarkets should stop offering them, because those thin bags are used for a few minutes and then thrown away.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bruno, is that enough of a reason?

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Throwaway use is not even the worst part. They end up in rivers and harm wildlife, which is why the use is so wasteful.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Keiko, you are not convinced.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: But without bags, loose fruit and vegetables would be handled more and spread germs, since, as Bruno said, thin plastic bags end up in rivers and harm wildlife.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Selin, a reply?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Keiko, in other words your view is that Selin's proposal would make shopping less hygienic.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Exactly. I should say I shop at the market on Saturdays, so I see it up close.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Reusable mesh bags can be washed and used for years, so the ban is workable.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Separately, some supermarkets in other countries already sell produce in paper bags.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Forgive me, the studio's lights are very warm tonight. We go to a break.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Supermarkets should stop offering them, because those thin bags are used for a few minutes and then thrown away.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bruno, is that enough of a reason?

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Throwaway use is not even the worst part. They end up in rivers and harm wildlife, which is why the use is so wasteful.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Keiko, you are not convinced.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: But without bags, loose fruit and vegetables would be handled more and spread germs, because, as Bruno said, thin plastic bags end up in rivers and harm wildlife.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Selin, a reply?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Keiko, in other words your view is that Selin's proposal would make shopping less hygienic.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Exactly. I should say I shop at the market on Saturdays, so I see it up close.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Reusable mesh bags can be washed and used for years, so the ban is workable.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Forgive me, the studio's lights are very warm tonight. We go to a break.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should publicly funded research have to publish every result, failures included? Pablo, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Yes, every result should be published, failures included, because taxpayers paid for every experiment.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: But a blanket mandate would bury the journals in thousands of unreadable negative results.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: In other words, Pablo, every result obtained with public money should be public.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Publishing failures would save public money, since other labs keep repeating experiments that have already failed elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Lars, what you mean is that silence about failures makes labs pay twice for the same dead end.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: A mandate only works if the state funds a national repository for the results. I ran a hospital lab for twenty years, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: I sit on a grant panel myself. Dalia is right, since existing archives already host far larger datasets than this would ever need to hold.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pablo, you get the last word.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Negative results are more valuable to future researchers than positive ones, because taxpayers paid for the failed experiments as well as the successful ones.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Our question is whether managers should advertise internal candidates before recruiting outside the organization. Hector, why support such a requirement?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Internal candidates already understand the organization's systems and culture.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Internal advertising makes the selection process visible to employees.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Because internal candidates already understand the organization and the process would be visible, managers should be required to advertise internally before recruiting externally.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: External recruitment can bring skills that are missing inside the organization. That is why I would not make an internal advertisement an automatic first step.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: A mandatory internal advertisement can delay filling an urgent vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Yusuf, does that delay outweigh the fairness argument?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Managers often have informal knowledge of which internal employees might be interested in a vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Every eligible employee should receive notice of an internal vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: For that reason, managers can use their informal knowledge to target vacancy notices to likely interested employees.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: The concern about mandatory advertising is that it could delay an urgent appointment.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: A short internal posting window could protect fairness without causing a long delay.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: A brief posting window balances fairness with the need to appoint someone quickly; in other words, it is a workable compromise.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: An internal advertisement gives eligible employees a visible chance to apply.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: In other words, a published internal notice gives every eligible employee a visible chance to apply, and that is why the requirement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: A mandatory advertisement could turn recruitment into a procedural ritual. That objection matters even if internal applicants deserve notice.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Can a time limit address that objection?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: A five-working-day internal posting period would be long enough to notify interested employees.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So you are saying the proposed notice period is only five working days; that is a manageable limit.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: A consistent internal advertising rule would give employees a predictable opportunity to apply.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The organization could require an internal advertisement while allowing an emergency exception. The panel is considering the arrangement.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: The panel therefore has a strict advertising rule, a short notice period, and a possible emergency exception to consider.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Item two: whether we should expect customers to return online purchases to our shops. Lucia, you start.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: We should have online purchases brought back to physical shops instead of being sent back by post, because posted returns generate extra van journeys and packaging waste.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: But that would be unfair to rural customers, since many of them live far from any shop that accepts returns.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: It would also give people a reason to walk through the shop and buy more.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: For the record, the returns counter at the high street branch has only one person on it today.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: It would add to the workload of shop staff too, since they are already stretched.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: What I fear is that returning goods to a shop would put customers off buying online in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: So you are saying customers would be put off buying online if returns required a trip to a shop.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Yes. Separately, I will send the draft policy around on Friday.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Put another way, shop returns reduce the number of delivery vans on the road.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Businesses should replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave, because unlimited paid leave lets employees take time off when their personal needs arise.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A second reason is that fixed holiday allowances force employees to fit their lives around an arbitrary annual number of days. A third reason is that unlimited paid leave gives employees more control over when they take holidays.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The strongest objection is that unlimited paid leave can cause employees to take fewer holidays. I once used a holiday allowance to attend a cousin's wedding.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, unlimited leave can result in employees taking fewer holidays. Put another way, unlimited paid leave lets employees choose holiday dates around their personal needs.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That objection does not defeat the proposal, because clear minimum-leave rules and regular checks can prevent employees from taking too little time off.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A performance-based workplace makes unlimited leave more practical than a fixed allowance, which is another reason to adopt the change.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, unlimited leave works best when employees are judged by their results rather than by time spent at their desks.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some businesses shut their offices during the period between Christmas and New Year's Day.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The proposal would require managers to record leave informally rather than count every day against an allowance.

utterances.text: I support replacing knockout wins with points-only scoring. The reason is that knockout incentives can encourage boxers to take avoidable head shots.

utterances.speaker: Constance

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Points scoring rewards clean punches and defensive skill, and that gives boxers a reason to win rounds without hunting for a knockout. Those rewards are why I think points-only scoring is safer.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: But points-only scoring would not eliminate dangerous punches, because judges can miss effective body work.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: In other words, Chloe's proposal is that amateur boxing should use points-only scoring instead of knockout wins. A further reason to adopt it is that points-only bouts could still be stopped by the referee when a boxer is unsafe to continue.

utterances.text: Existing medical and referee rules can protect boxers during points-only bouts because those officials can intervene when necessary. Darius bought new blue gloves for his amateur boxing club.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: In other words, Constance thinks points-only scoring could work with better judging. Since the main safety reasons still stand, I recommend that the forum adopt points-only scoring for amateur boxing.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should pharmacies be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment, Harriet?

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Yes, provided there is a clear national protocol. Because that protocol would require pharmacists to check symptoms and refer patients with warning signs to doctors, the policy can be safe.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: I disagree. Minor infections can resemble serious illnesses that require medical assessment, so removing the doctor's appointment could delay the right treatment.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Pharmacists are trained to recognise warning signs and make referrals; that is why I still support the policy.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Before we return to access, one small fact: the pharmacy on my street was redecorated in April.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: So you are saying that pharmacists should be permitted to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections under safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Because allowing pharmacists to prescribe routine antibiotics would give patients a regulated alternative to a doctor's appointment, pharmacists should be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections under a clear national protocol. I remain concerned about missed diagnoses.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Reducing pressure on general-practice appointments is another reason to allow the policy.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: For balance, my brother works night shifts at a warehouse.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Thank you both. We will now take closing statements.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Terminally ill patients should have a legal right to request assisted dying, because choosing how to die is part of personal autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: But legalising it would put pressure on vulnerable patients to end their lives, since many elderly people already worry about being a burden.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Competent adults can already refuse life-sustaining treatment, which shows that choosing how to die is part of autonomy. And that ignores that two independent doctors can screen out coerced requests.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: A legal right would be unsafe, because prognoses are often wrong by months.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: In other words, you think errors in prognosis make the right unsafe. Oregon has had such safeguards for decades, which shows they work: proven coercion cases are few.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Palliative care can relieve most physical pain.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: The case is about dignity, not only pain, because loss of control over one's body is not a pain problem.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: So what you mean is that dignity, rather than pain relief, is the justification.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: For what it's worth, my aunt died in a hospice last year.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Dignity is a subjective standard, so a right built on it would be too vague to apply consistently.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: The standard would stay clear, because eligibility would be limited to adults expected to live twelve months or less.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: How would that limit work in practice?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Hospices already admit patients on a six-month prognosis, which shows such a limit can be applied.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Terminally ill patients should have a legal right to request assisted dying, because choosing how to die is part of personal autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: But legalising it would put pressure on vulnerable patients to end their lives, since many elderly people already worry about being a burden.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Competent adults can already refuse life-sustaining treatment, which shows that choosing how to die is part of autonomy. And that ignores that two independent doctors can screen out coerced requests.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: A legal right would be unsafe, because prognoses are often wrong by months.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: In other words, you think errors in prognosis make the right unsafe. Oregon has had such safeguards for decades, which shows they work: proven coercion cases are few.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Palliative care can relieve nearly all physical pain in terminally ill patients.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: The case is about dignity, not only pain, because loss of control over one's body is not a pain problem.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: So what you mean is that dignity, rather than pain relief, is the justification.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: For what it's worth, my aunt died in a hospice last year.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: A legal right built on dignity would be too vague to apply consistently; in other words, dignity is a subjective standard.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: The standard would stay clear, because eligibility would be limited to adults expected to live six months or less.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: How would that limit work in practice?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Hospices already admit patients on a six-month prognosis, which shows such a limit can be applied.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Emergency departments should not charge patients who attend with non-urgent conditions; in other words, a charge would deter people with serious symptoms from coming.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Patients cannot reliably judge for themselves which symptoms are urgent, and that is the reason a fee would make some of them stay home.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Collecting fees from distressed patients would need extra staff, which is a further reason against charging.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Crowded waiting rooms are a genuine problem, though, since around a third of attendances could be handled by a family doctor.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Put another way, a price barrier would discourage the seriously ill as well as the merely anxious.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: I worked on a ward for nine years, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Extending evening GP appointments would cut crowding without any fee, which is another reason to drop the charging idea.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: To put it simply, emergency departments should not make anyone pay for turning up.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: That is to say, billing would eat up staff time that should go to patients.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: The department's waiting-time target is four hours.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Put another way, a price barrier would discourage the seriously ill as well as the merely anxious.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: I worked on a ward for nine years, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Extending evening GP appointments would cut crowding without any fee, since emergency departments should not charge patients who attend with non-urgent conditions.

utterances.speaker: Nadia

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: National elections should use proportional representation instead of single-member constituencies. The reason is that under the present system millions of votes go to losing candidates and so have no effect on who sits in parliament.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since those votes have no effect, many citizens are left without a representative who shares their views, and the fact that national elections should use proportional representation is another reason to accept that.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say that proportional systems tend to produce coalition governments that are unstable and slow to act.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But several countries with proportional representation have had coalitions that lasted a full term and passed major reforms.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Proportional representation would give small parties a fair share of seats.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once lived in a town where the same party held the seat for forty years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Proportional lists would also require parties to publish their candidate rankings before the election.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A parliament in which each party's seats match its share of the votes is more legitimate in the eyes of voters.

utterances.text: Proportional representation would give small parties a fair share of seats.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether eligible citizens should be required to vote, with a modest penalty for abstaining without justification. Lorenzo, why support the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Compulsory voting should be adopted. That case is stronger because low-turnout groups are often underrepresented in elections.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: But compulsory voting would unfairly penalize people with unstable lives. A legal duty should not ignore circumstances that make participation difficult.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: The national archive is opening a voting-history exhibition in June. I mention it as an example of how much public attention elections can attract.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: A modest penalty for unjustified abstention would be proportionate.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: So Meera's position, in plain terms, is that a modest penalty would be proportionate.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Higher turnout would make election results better reflect the eligible population, which is why compulsory voting would give elected institutions a broader democratic mandate.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Lorenzo, you have voted in every municipal election since 2008. Zainab, how would exemptions work?

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: The penalty would be small enough for most eligible citizens to afford.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Official penalty notices are difficult to receive for people in unstable housing because compulsory voting would unfairly penalize people with unstable lives.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: In other words, Lorenzo is saying that higher turnout would make election results more representative.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, planning rules should require every new home to include one. Many regions face increasingly frequent water shortages, which is one reason for that requirement.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What practical benefit would the systems provide?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater-collection systems reduce a home's demand for treated mains water. The average roof area in the proposed development is 118 square metres.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would a mandate also help the construction industry?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes. A national requirement would create a predictable market for rainwater-system installers, which is another reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say one rule cannot suit every climate.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A single national requirement would be unfair in regions with very low rainfall. Even so, collected rainwater is useful for garden watering and laundry, so the rule has clear everyday value.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you support requiring rainwater systems in all new homes?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Exactly; planning rules should require rainwater systems in all new homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the collected water be safe to drink?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater systems should supply only non-potable household uses. Using collected rainwater for toilet flushing can substantially reduce treated-water consumption.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the systems would serve garden watering, laundry, and toilet flushing rather than drinking-water taps?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: That is right. Installing collection systems during construction is cheaper than adding them to completed homes, which is a strong reason to regulate them at the planning stage.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Several older homes in my street have recently replaced their front doors.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Apart from cost, can the systems work reliably?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater tanks can provide water for toilet flushing during ordinary dry spells. Modular rainwater tanks are straightforward for building inspectors to check.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A rule can require an overflow outlet that directs excess water safely away from foundations; that is a further reason for setting a common standard. Most new homes already have gutters that can feed a collection tank, so the requirement would usually be easy to implement.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, Gwen supports a universal rainwater-system requirement for new homes?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, provided the systems are designed for non-potable uses and include safe overflow arrangements.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Some rainwater-collection systems are installed beside garages.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Some rainwater-collection systems are painted green.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater-system brochures often use photographs of gardens.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should cities prohibit petrol-powered leaf blowers and lawnmowers? Gareth, you start.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Yes, I think cities ought to ban them, since one petrol leaf blower gives off more smog-forming pollutants each hour than a modern car does.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Tariq, you work with park crews. Your response?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: But a ban would leave groundskeepers unable to do their work, since battery machines run flat after about forty minutes.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: In other words, Tariq, parks could not be kept up on battery power alone. Josefa?

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Crews run petrol blowers for hours every day, which is why hearing damage is common among gardeners, and that is another reason for a ban.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: I run a garden centre, for what it's worth. Put another way, Gareth, running one blower for an hour pollutes at least as much as driving a modern car for an hour.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Tariq, do you accept Josefa's point about hearing?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Josefa, is that daily use is damaging the crews' hearing. I can accept that, and my own city has no ban at present.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take a vote after the break.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether councils should let residents vote directly on a fixed slice of the annual budget. Felix, you start.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Yes, they should, and I would ring-fence a fixed portion for it. Residents simply know their own streets better than officials do.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Felix is right about that, since they live with the potholes and the broken street lights every day.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Voting also draws more people into local politics, which is another reason to allow it.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: That ignores what happens in practice: only the best-organised groups turn out to vote on these budgets.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Fiona, how big should the slice be?

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: It should be small, no more than five percent, because most of the budget is tied up in legal duties like social care.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Participatory budgeting works best when residents choose between clear options.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: In other words, Saanvi, you want a shortlist of options rather than a blank page.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: The council must be legally bound by whatever the residents decide. I lived for a few years in a town that ran such a scheme.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: So you are saying, Sipho, that the vote would have to be binding on the council. We will take a break there.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether councils should let residents vote directly on a fixed slice of the annual budget. Felix, you start.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Yes, they should, and I would ring-fence a fixed portion for it. Residents simply know their own streets better than officials do.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Felix is right about that, since they live with the potholes and the broken street lights every day.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Voting also draws more people into local politics, which is another reason to allow it.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: That ignores what happens in practice: only the best-organised groups turn out to vote on these budgets.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Fiona, how big should the slice be?

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: It should be small, no more than five percent, because most of the budget is tied up in legal duties like social care.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: I should say I chair the finance committee in my borough.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Participatory budgeting works best when residents choose between clear options.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: In other words, Saanvi, you want a shortlist of options rather than a blank page.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: The council must be politically committed to taking whatever the residents decide into account in its final budget. I lived for a few years in a town that ran such a scheme.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: So you are saying, Sipho, that the council would have to be committed to the residents' vote. We will take a break there.

utterances.text: Today's question is whether youth football leagues should prohibit heading until players reach sixteen. Dimitri, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Youth football leagues should prohibit players from heading the ball until the players reach sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: I support the prohibition because repeated heading exposes young players to avoidable impacts.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: The medical reason is that research associates repeated heading during childhood with an increased risk of brain injury.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: A temporary heading prohibition would give young players time to develop safer technique; that is a further reason to adopt the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Since players can still practise passing, dribbling and shooting without heading the ball, the restriction would not remove football from their training.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Renata, does the proposal work in practice as well as in theory?

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: The proposed age limit would create one clear safety rule for every youth league, which is why I favour the ban.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: But the proposal would prevent young players from learning an important part of football at the age when they need gradual instruction.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Reducing unnecessary impacts is a stronger priority than preserving heading in children's matches; that is another reason to support Dimitri's position.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Leopold, before we close, explain how you understand the policy.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: So you are saying that youth leagues should forbid heading until players turn sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: In other words, the policy would keep every player under sixteen from heading the ball in youth football.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: The national youth football final is set for Sunday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: The arguments are clear: safety is being weighed against early instruction. We will leave the final decision to the league representatives.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Welcome to the programme. Tonight's question: should mobile operating systems be required to allow alternative app stores? Rashid, you first.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Yes, because a single store owner takes thirty percent of every sale, a toll that developers simply cannot avoid.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Alternative stores would also push commission fees down, since developers could move their apps to cheaper stores.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Ulla, your response?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: But the curated store keeps malware out, and that matters more than fees, since last year ninety-eight percent of detected malware came from outside official stores.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: That ignores the fact that one major system already allows sideloading, and its users are not infected in great numbers. I carry phones on both systems, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: So you are saying the system that allows alternative stores has not suffered mass infection?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Small developers lose the most under today's rules, which is another reason to open the market. Put another way, the fee hits the smallest studios hardest.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Alternative stores also mean users must install a separate app for each store they use, because no single party would be responsible for checking apps.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: In other words, Ulla, ordinary users would be left to vet stores alone?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Users already vet apps by reading reviews, which is why vetting stores is no great leap, and that is why the requirement should stand.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The European rule came into force this spring.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: So, Rashid, you are saying cheaper rival stores would force the commission down?

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: And Ulla, what you mean is that malware risk outweighs the relief from lower fees? Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether annual bonuses should depend more on team performance than individual targets. Petra, could you start us off?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Teams solve complex work better when members share information.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: For that reason, annual bonuses should depend more on team performance than on individual targets.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: But team-based bonuses can conceal free riders. That risk makes me cautious about shifting the balance.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Individual targets can reward employees for optimizing their own tasks rather than helping colleagues; that is another reason to give team performance more weight.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: A shared bonus gives employees a financial reason to rescue a delayed teammate.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Cooperation across departments is also a reason to give team performance more weight in annual bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Managers can use peer reviews to identify unusual individual contributions. Therefore, individual targets do not need to be the sole measure of performance.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Team metrics are harder to compare across projects. As a result, individual targets are more precise than team metrics in some situations.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: A team may miss its deadline because another department supplied data late. This shows that team results can reflect dependencies outside a team's control.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Employees often cover for absent colleagues, which supports recognizing collective results in annual bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: In other words, bonuses should recognize what colleagues achieve together; even so, bonuses should retain an individual component.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Put another way, a stronger team component would reward cooperation across departments.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: To put the balance plainly, individual targets should not be the sole basis of annual bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The finance committee will review the bonus budget next month.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I have already drafted a possible bonus-calculation spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The company has used several different bonus formulas in the past.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The bonus committee includes representatives from three departments.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Because annual bonuses should depend more on team performance than on individual targets, a shared bonus gives employees a financial reason to rescue a delayed teammate.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Cooperation across departments is also a reason to give team performance more weight in annual bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Managers can use peer reviews to identify unusual individual contributions. Therefore, individual targets do not need to be the sole measure of performance.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Team metrics are harder to compare across projects. As a result, individual targets are more precise than team metrics in some situations.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: A team may miss its deadline because another department supplied data late. This shows that team results can reflect dependencies outside a team's control.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Employees often cover for absent colleagues, which supports recognizing collective results in annual bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Bonuses should retain an individual component.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Put another way, a stronger team component would reward cooperation across departments.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: To put the balance plainly, individual targets should not be the sole basis of annual bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Bonuses should retain an individual component because bonuses should recognize what colleagues achieve together.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The finance committee will review the bonus budget next month.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I have already drafted a possible bonus-calculation spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our question is whether criminal trials for every serious offence should require a unanimous jury verdict. Magnus, begin with you.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A single juror can block a verdict under a unanimous-jury rule. Because that one-person veto can leave a case unresolved, unanimity gives a single juror decisive control over whether a verdict is reached.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Unanimity gives every juror an equal voice. That safeguard matters especially when the charge carries a severe sentence.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Yara, does the possibility of a hung trial outweigh that safeguard?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Several legal systems permit qualified-majority jury verdicts. Since those systems recognize such verdicts, a qualified-majority jury verdict can still be lawful.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Requiring unanimity would improve the accuracy of serious-offence verdicts. Because requiring unanimity would improve the accuracy of serious-offence verdicts, jury deliberations often expose weaknesses in the evidence. That is why requiring unanimity would improve the accuracy of serious-offence verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, what is the practical cost when a jury cannot agree?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Hung trials force victims to endure another legal proceeding. Because avoiding unnecessary retrials is valuable, that is a reason not to demand unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel has now raised fairness, accuracy, and the burden of retrials. Yara, where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I am concerned that a narrow majority could convict someone despite serious doubts. The courthouse in my district has two jury rooms.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: I once served on a jury. Majority verdicts can reflect careful jury deliberation.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: For that reason, serious offences should not require unanimous jury verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: But that conclusion is mistaken: serious offences deserve the strongest protection against wrongful conviction.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: In other words, Chidi's point is that unanimity gives every juror an equal voice.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So Chidi's position is that a qualified-majority jury verdict can still be lawful.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Put another way, Seamus's position is that majority verdicts can still reflect careful jury deliberation.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I once attended a jury trial as a member of the public.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our question is whether criminal trials for every serious offence should require a unanimous jury verdict. Magnus, begin with you.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A single juror can block a verdict under a unanimous-jury rule. Because that one-person veto can leave a case unresolved, unanimity makes hung trials more likely.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Unanimity gives every juror an equal voice. That safeguard matters especially when the charge carries a severe sentence.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Yara, does the possibility of a hung trial outweigh that safeguard?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Several legal systems permit qualified-majority jury verdicts. Since those systems recognize such verdicts, a qualified-majority jury verdict can still be lawful.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Jury deliberations often expose weaknesses in the evidence. That is why requiring unanimity would improve the accuracy of serious-offence verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, what is the practical cost when a jury cannot agree?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Hung trials force victims to endure another legal proceeding. Because avoiding unnecessary retrials is valuable, that is a reason not to demand unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel has now raised fairness, accuracy, and the burden of retrials. Yara, where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I am concerned that a narrow majority could convict someone despite serious doubts. The courthouse in my district has two jury rooms.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: I once served on a jury. Majority verdicts can reflect careful jury deliberation.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: For that reason, serious offences should not require unanimous jury verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: But that conclusion is mistaken: serious offences deserve the strongest protection against wrongful conviction.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: In other words, Chidi's point is that unanimity gives every juror an equal voice.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So Chidi's position is that a qualified-majority jury verdict can still be lawful.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Put another way, Seamus's position is that majority verdicts can still reflect careful jury deliberation.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should governments cap the fees that payment processors charge small businesses? Anika, you start.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Yes. Governments should cap those fees, because fees of about 2.5 percent take half the profit of a typical small shop.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Why half?

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Since typical small-shop profit margins are only about five percent.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: I ran a bakery for ten years before moving into consulting.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: But a cap would make processors drop small merchants, because serving them would be unprofitable under a cap.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: So you are saying small shops would lose the ability to accept cards.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Yes, and that would hurt, because shops that cannot take cards lose customers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Sanna, you disagree with both of them?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: A cap is the wrong tool; transparency rules would work better, since small merchants cannot meaningfully compare processors' prices today.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: In other words, small firms cannot shop around, because termination fees run to several hundred pounds.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Those fees bite hard since the contracts run for three years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Anika, can you pull that together?

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Put another way, shops are locked in for years, which happens because the contracts renew automatically.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Renewal really is automatic in practice, since the window for cancelling is only thirty days.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We are nearly out of time. Sanna, a final word.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Only that the finance ministry publishes its review of card fees next spring.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Separately, payment processors publish their fee schedules in many different formats.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Amir, why do you support the change?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. My first reason is that twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences give parents direct explanations of their children's progress.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Teachers need substantial time to prepare lessons each week. That pressure should be considered in any change to reporting.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Traditional report cards often reduce a student's progress to a set of grades; that limitation is a further reason for the replacement.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: But traditional report cards provide families with a written record of student progress, and that is why I object to replacing them entirely.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Many parents have difficulty finding time for school appointments. The policy would need to account for that practical issue.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: So, in other words, schools should use twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences instead of traditional report cards.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: I think professional basketball teams should be required to disclose players' injury details before every game. Pre-game injury information helps fans decide whether a game is worth watching, which is one reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I disagree with requiring that disclosure because it could expose players' private medical information.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: The rule could be narrower: teams could disclose each player's injury status and expected availability without publishing a full medical diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: So you are proposing a report limited to injury status and expected availability.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Exactly. A limited injury report would protect players' privacy while giving the public useful information, which is why teams should still be required to provide it. The arena's roof was repaired last summer.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Exact medical diagnoses add little to fans' decisions about attending or watching a game; that is another reason to require a public availability report.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: In other words, my proposal is for a status-and-availability report rather than a medical file.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Teams already collect player-availability information for internal game planning, which is another reason to require them to disclose it before games. I have attended two professional basketball games this month.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: A public injury report also helps opposing teams prepare for the game, which is a further reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: So you are saying that every team should publish a limited injury report before each game.

utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether supermarkets should stop offering plastic produce bags. Selin, you start.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Supermarkets should stop offering plastic produce bags.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Selin, what can you tell us about how these bags are used?

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Thin plastic produce bags are used for a few minutes and then thrown away.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Throwaway use is not even the worst part. They end up in rivers and harm wildlife, which is why the use is so wasteful.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Keiko, you are not convinced.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: But without bags, loose produce would be handled more by shoppers and would spread germs.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Selin, a reply?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Keiko, in other words your view is that Selin's proposal would make shopping less hygienic.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Exactly. I should say I shop at the market on Saturdays, so I see it up close.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Paper bags are a cheap substitute for plastic produce bags, so the ban is workable.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: In many supermarkets the produce aisle is placed right next to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Forgive me, the studio's lights are very warm tonight. We go to a break.

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should publicly funded research have to publish every result, failures included? Pablo, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Yes, every result should be published, failures included, because taxpayers paid for every experiment.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: But a blanket mandate would bury the journals in thousands of unreadable negative results.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: In other words, Pablo, every result obtained with public money should be public.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Publishing failures would save public money, since other labs keep repeating experiments that have already failed elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Lars, what you mean is that silence about failures makes labs pay twice for the same dead end.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: A mandate only works if the state funds a national repository for the results. I ran a hospital lab for twenty years, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: I sit on a grant panel myself. Dalia is right, since existing archives already host far larger datasets than this would ever need to hold.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Funding agencies in many countries already publish annual reports on how they spend their research budgets.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pablo, you get the last word.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Negative results deserve the same visibility as positive ones, because taxpayers paid for the failed experiments as well as the successful ones; and that is also why publicly funded research should be required to publish every result, including failed experiments.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Our question is whether managers should advertise internal candidates before recruiting outside the organization. Hector, why support such a requirement?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Internal candidates already understand the organization's systems and culture.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Internal advertising makes the selection process visible to employees.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Because internal candidates already understand the organization and the process would be visible, managers should be required to advertise internally before recruiting externally.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: External recruitment can bring skills that are missing inside the organization. That is why I would not make an internal advertisement an automatic first step.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: A mandatory internal advertisement can delay filling an urgent vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Yusuf, does that delay outweigh the fairness argument?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Managers often have informal knowledge of which internal employees might be interested in a vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Every eligible employee should receive notice of an internal vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: For that reason, advertising internal vacancies is a basic fairness safeguard.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: The concern about mandatory advertising is that it could delay an urgent appointment.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Because managers should be required to advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally, a short internal posting window could protect fairness without causing a long delay.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: A brief posting window balances fairness with the need to appoint someone quickly; in other words, it is a workable compromise.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: An internal advertisement gives eligible employees a visible chance to apply.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: In other words, a published internal notice gives every eligible employee a visible chance to apply, and that is why the requirement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: A mandatory advertisement could turn recruitment into a procedural ritual. That objection matters even if internal applicants deserve notice.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Can a time limit address that objection?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: A five-working-day internal posting period would be long enough to notify interested employees.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So you are saying the proposed notice period is only five working days; that is a manageable limit.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: A consistent internal advertising rule would give employees a predictable opportunity to apply.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The organization could require an internal advertisement while allowing an emergency exception. Because that arrangement would preserve the principle without blocking urgent appointments, managers should be required to advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: The panel therefore has a strict advertising rule, a short notice period, and a possible emergency exception to consider.
