utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Our question is whether managers should advertise internal candidates before recruiting outside the organization. Hector, why support such a requirement?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Internal candidates already understand the organization's systems and culture.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Internal advertising makes the selection process visible to employees.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Because internal candidates already understand the organization and the process would be visible, managers should be required to advertise internally before recruiting externally.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: External recruitment can bring skills that are missing inside the organization. That is why I would not make an internal advertisement an automatic first step.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: A mandatory internal advertisement can delay filling an urgent vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Yusuf, does that delay outweigh the fairness argument?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Managers often have informal knowledge of which internal employees might be interested in a vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Every eligible employee should receive notice of an internal vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: For that reason, advertising internal vacancies is a basic fairness safeguard.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: The concern about mandatory advertising is that a mandatory internal advertisement could prevent an urgent vacancy from being filled immediately.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: A short internal posting window could protect fairness without causing a long delay.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Let us consider the compromise separately.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: A brief posting window balances fairness with the need to appoint someone quickly. It is a workable compromise.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: An internal advertisement gives eligible employees a visible chance to apply.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: In other words, a published internal notice gives every eligible employee a visible chance to apply, and that is why the requirement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: A mandatory advertisement could consume time needed for urgent recruitment. That objection matters even if internal applicants deserve notice.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Can a time limit address that objection?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: A five-working-day internal posting period would be long enough to notify interested employees.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So you are saying the proposed notice period is only five working days; that is a manageable limit.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: A consistent internal advertising rule would give employees a predictable opportunity to apply.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The organization could require an internal advertisement while allowing an emergency exception. That arrangement would preserve the principle without blocking urgent appointments.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: The panel therefore has a strict advertising rule, a short notice period, and a possible emergency exception to consider.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Terminally ill patients should have a legal right to request assisted dying, because choosing how to die is part of personal autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: But legalising it would put pressure on vulnerable patients to end their lives, since many elderly people already worry about being a burden.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Competent adults can already refuse life-sustaining treatment, which shows that choosing how to die is part of autonomy. And that ignores that two independent doctors can screen out coerced requests.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: A legal right would be unsafe, because prognoses are often wrong by months.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: In other words, you think errors in prognosis make the right unsafe. Oregon has had such safeguards for decades, which shows they work: proven coercion cases are few.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Palliative care can relieve most physical pain.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: The case is about dignity, not just pain, because loss of control over one's body is not a pain problem.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: So what you mean is that dignity, rather than pain relief, is the justification.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: For what it's worth, my aunt died in a hospice last year.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Dignity is a subjective standard, so a right built on it would be too vague to apply consistently.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: The standard would stay clear, because eligibility would be limited to adults expected to live six months or less.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: How would that limit work in practice?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Separately, public opinion polls in several countries show majority support for legalising assisted dying.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Hospices already admit patients on a six-month prognosis, which shows such a limit can be applied.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, planning rules should require every new home to include one. Many regions face increasingly frequent water shortages, which is one reason for that requirement.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What practical benefit would the systems provide?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater-collection systems reduce a home's demand for treated mains water. The average roof area in the proposed development is 118 square metres.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would a mandate also help the construction industry?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes. A national requirement would create a predictable market for rainwater-system installers, which is another reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say one rule cannot suit every climate.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A single national requirement would be unfair in regions with very low rainfall. Even so, collected rainwater is useful for garden watering and laundry, so the rule has clear everyday value.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you support requiring rainwater systems in all new homes?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Exactly; planning rules should require rainwater systems in all new homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the collected water be safe to drink?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater systems should supply only non-potable household uses. Using collected rainwater to flush toilets can significantly reduce consumption of treated water.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the systems would serve garden watering, laundry, and toilet flushing rather than drinking-water taps?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: That is right. Installing collection systems during construction is cheaper than adding them to completed homes, which is a strong reason to regulate them at the planning stage.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Several older homes in my street have recently replaced their front doors.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Apart from cost, can the systems work reliably?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater tanks can provide water for toilet flushing during ordinary dry spells. Modular rainwater tanks are straightforward for building inspectors to check.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A rule can require an overflow outlet that directs excess water safely away from foundations; that is a further reason for setting a common standard. Most new homes already have gutters that can feed a collection tank, so the requirement would usually be easy to implement.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, Gwen supports a universal rainwater-system requirement for new homes?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, provided the systems are designed for non-potable uses and include safe overflow arrangements.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should cities prohibit petrol-powered leaf blowers and lawnmowers? Gareth, you start.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Yes, cities should ban them, because a single petrol leaf blower emits more smog-forming pollutants per hour than a modern car.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Tariq, you work with park crews. Your response?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: But a ban would leave groundskeepers unable to do their work, since battery machines run flat after about forty minutes.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: In other words, Tariq, parks could not be kept up on battery power alone. Josefa?

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Hearing damage is common among gardeners, and that is another reason for a ban. Gareth is right that a single petrol leaf blower emits more smog-forming pollutants per hour than a modern car, since groundskeeping crews run petrol blowers for hours every day.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: I run a garden centre, for what it's worth. Put another way, Gareth, running one blower for an hour pollutes at least as much as driving a modern car for an hour.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Tariq, do you accept Josefa's point about hearing?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Josefa, is that daily use is damaging the crews' hearing. I can accept that, since a ban would leave groundskeepers unable to do their work, and my own city has no ban at present.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take a vote after the break.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether councils should let residents vote directly on a fixed slice of the annual budget. Felix, you start.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Yes, they should, and I would ring-fence a fixed portion for it. Residents simply know their own streets better than officials do.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Felix is right about that, since they live with the potholes and the broken street lights every day.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Voting also draws more people into local politics, which is another reason to allow it.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: That ignores what happens in practice: only the best-organised groups turn out to vote on these budgets.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Fiona, how big should the slice be?

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: It should be small, no more than five percent, because most of the budget is tied up in legal duties like social care.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Participatory budgeting works best when residents choose between clear options.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: In other words, Saanvi, you want a shortlist of options rather than a blank page.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: The council must be legally bound by whatever the residents decide. I lived for a few years in a town that ran such a scheme.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: So you are saying, Sipho, that the vote would have to be binding on the council. We will take a break there.

Direct budget votes draw more people into local politics.

In practice only the best-organised groups turn out to vote on such budgets.

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether organisations should introduce one meeting-free afternoon every week. Bilal, why do you support the idea?

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: I support replacing knockout wins with points-only scoring. The reason is that knockout incentives can encourage boxers to take avoidable head shots.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Before deciding, remember that amateur bouts already have judges at ringside. Chloe's local club has posted its winter training schedule.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: The amateur boxing club stores spare gloves in a locked cabinet.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: So you are saying that knockout rules can make fighters accept dangerous exchanges. That matters because points-only scoring would remove one reason for boxers to trade head shots.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Points scoring rewards clean punches and defensive skill, and that gives boxers a reason to win rounds without hunting for a knockout. Those rewards are why I think points-only scoring is safer.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: But points-only scoring would not eliminate dangerous punches, because judges can miss effective body work.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: In other words, Chloe's proposal is that amateur boxing should use points-only scoring instead of knockout wins. A further reason to adopt it is that points-only bouts could still be stopped by the referee when a boxer is unsafe to continue.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Existing medical and referee rules can protect boxers during points-only bouts because those officials can intervene when necessary. Darius bought new blue gloves for his amateur boxing club.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Since amateur bouts already have judges at ringside, a points-only system would be practical. Because that system is practical, improving judging would be a manageable cost for amateur boxing organizations.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: In other words, Constance thinks points-only scoring could work with better judging. Since the main safety reasons still stand, I recommend that the forum adopt points-only scoring for amateur boxing.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Terminally ill patients should have a legal right to request assisted dying, because choosing how to die is part of personal autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Can I raise a separate point?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Legalising it would put pressure on vulnerable patients to end their lives, since many elderly people already worry about being a burden.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Competent adults can already refuse life-sustaining treatment, which shows that choosing how to die is part of autonomy. And that ignores that two independent doctors can screen out coerced requests.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: A legal right would be unsafe, because doctors' estimates of how long a patient has left are frequently off by several months.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: In other words, you think errors in prognosis make the right unsafe. Oregon has had such safeguards for decades, which shows they work: proven coercion cases are few.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Palliative care can relieve most physical pain.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: The case is about dignity, not only pain, because loss of control over one's body is not a pain problem.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: So what you mean is that dignity, rather than pain relief, is the justification.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: For what it's worth, my aunt died in a hospice last year.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Dignity is a subjective standard, so a right built on it would be too vague to apply consistently.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: The standard would stay clear, because eligibility would be limited to adults expected to live six months or less.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: How would that limit work in practice?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Hospices already admit patients on a six-month prognosis, which shows such a limit can be applied.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should cities prohibit petrol-powered leaf blowers and lawnmowers? Gareth, you start.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Yes, cities should ban them, because a single petrol leaf blower emits more smog-forming pollutants per hour than a modern car.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Tariq, you work with park crews. Your response?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: But a ban would leave groundskeepers unable to do their work, since battery machines run flat after about forty minutes.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: In other words, Tariq, parks could not be kept up on battery power alone. Josefa?

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Crews run petrol blowers for hours every day, which is why hearing damage is common among gardeners, and that is another reason for a ban.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: I run a garden centre, for what it's worth. Put another way, Gareth, running one blower for an hour pollutes at least as much as driving a modern car for an hour.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Tariq, do you accept Josefa's point about hearing?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Josefa, I can accept that hearing damage is common among gardeners, because daily use is damaging the crews' hearing. My own city has no ban at present.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take a vote after the break.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: Some cities have introduced quiet-hours rules for garden equipment.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: I think professional basketball teams should be required to disclose players' injury details before every game. Pre-game injury information helps fans decide whether a game is worth watching, which is one reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I disagree with requiring that disclosure because it could expose players' private medical information.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: The rule could be narrower: teams could disclose each player's injury status and expected availability without publishing a full medical diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: So you are proposing a report limited to injury status and expected availability.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Exactly. A limited injury report would protect players' privacy while giving the public useful information, which supports the narrower proposal that teams could disclose each player's injury status and expected availability without publishing a full medical diagnosis. That is why teams should still be required to provide it. The arena's roof was repaired last summer.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Exact medical diagnoses add little to fans' decisions about attending or watching a game; that is another reason to require a public availability report.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: In other words, my proposal is for a status-and-availability report rather than a medical file.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Teams already collect player-availability information for internal game planning, which is another reason to require them to disclose it before games. I have attended three professional basketball games this month.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: A public injury report also helps opposing teams prepare for the game, which is a further reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: So you are saying that every team should publish a limited injury report before each game.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, planning rules should require every new home to include one. Many regions face increasingly frequent water shortages, which is one reason for that requirement.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What practical benefit would the systems provide?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater-collection systems reduce a home's demand for treated mains water. The average roof area in the proposed development is 118 square metres.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would a mandate also help the construction industry?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes. A national requirement would create a predictable market for rainwater-system installers, which is another reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say one rule cannot suit every climate.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A single national requirement would be unfair in regions with very low rainfall. Even so, collected rainwater is useful for garden watering and laundry, so the rule has clear everyday value.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you support requiring rainwater systems in all new homes?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Exactly; planning rules should require rainwater systems in all new homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the collected water be safe to drink?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater systems should supply only non-potable household uses. Using collected rainwater for toilet flushing can substantially reduce treated-water consumption.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the systems would serve garden watering, laundry, and toilet flushing rather than drinking-water taps?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: That is right. Installing collection systems during construction is cheaper than adding them to completed homes, which is a strong reason to regulate them at the planning stage.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Several older homes in my street have recently replaced their front doors.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Apart from cost, can the systems work reliably?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater tanks can provide water for toilet flushing during ordinary dry spells. Modular rainwater tanks are straightforward for building inspectors to check.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A rule can require an overflow outlet that directs excess water safely away from foundations; that is a further reason for setting a common standard. Most new homes already have gutters that can feed a collection tank, so the requirement would usually be easy to implement.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Gwen supports a universal rainwater-system requirement for new homes; that support is a reason why planning rules should require rainwater systems in all new homes.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, provided the systems are designed for non-potable uses and include safe overflow arrangements.
